recommendations.text: Create src/validation.js exporting validateEmail(value) and validateName(value). Each function must return null for valid input and the existing error message for invalid input.
Replace the duplicated email and name validation in createUser, updateUser, and inviteUser under src/handlers with calls to the shared validators.

Preserve each handler's observable behavior for the same inputs, including accepted and rejected values, exact error messages, validation order, and handling of missing or optional fields. Do not introduce normalization or new validation rules.
Add direct tests for both shared validators covering valid and invalid inputs, exact error messages, and boundary or unusual input cases identified in the existing validation logic.
Keep all existing tests passing and run npm test, the test command identified in the supplied repository snapshot, including the new module tests.

Compare the three existing implementations before extraction. Their source and behavioral equivalence are not established by the supplied snapshot metadata; any conflicting rules or error messages must be resolved without silently changing handler behavior.

Create src/validation.js exporting exactly validateEmail(value) and validateName(value). Each takes a single value and returns null when the value is valid, otherwise the existing error message string as currently produced by the handlers.

Remove the duplicated email and name validation from createUser, updateUser and inviteUser in src/handlers and have all three call the shared validators. No handler may retain its own private copy of the rules.

Observable handler behaviour must be identical before and after: same accepted and rejected inputs, same exact error message text, same error shape and status, same order in which email and name errors are reported, and same handling of missing, null, non-string or optional fields (for example updateUser possibly skipping validation for an absent field). Presence and optionality checks stay in the handler if that is where they live today.

Do not introduce trimming, case normalisation, stricter or looser patterns, new length limits, or reworded messages while extracting. The validators must be pure: no mutation of the input and no side effects.

Match the module system and export style already used by src/handlers (CommonJS or ES modules) and the existing test framework and test file layout, so that the new tests are picked up by npm test without configuration changes.

Before extracting, compare the three existing copies of the email and name validation line by line, including regexes, length bounds, type checks, treatment of empty and whitespace-only values, and message text. Record whether they are equivalent; this is the precondition for a single shared implementation.

The three copies may not be identical. If they differ in rules or messages, a single validateEmail(value) / validateName(value) cannot reproduce all three behaviours, and the requested signature conflicts with the requirement that behaviour not change. In that case implementation must stop at the divergence and surface it rather than silently choosing one variant, adding undisclosed parameters, or leaving a handler-specific rule behind.

The existing tests may not cover every validation branch in every handler, so a green run alone does not prove behaviour is unchanged. Where a handler's rejection paths and exact messages are not already asserted, add characterisation tests against the current code first, then refactor.

New tests exist for src/validation.js covering both functions: valid values return null, each distinct invalid case returns the exact existing message string, and the boundary cases present in the current logic (empty string, whitespace, undefined, null, non-string values, length limits) are asserted explicitly.
All pre-existing tests pass unmodified. An existing test may only be changed if it imports a helper that was moved, and never by altering an expected value or message.

Run npm test before the change to establish a baseline and after the change to confirm the full suite, including the new validation tests, passes. The snapshot declares no build, lint or typecheck command, so npm test is the only automated gate.

Confirm by search that no email or name validation logic (regexes, length checks, message literals) remains inside src/handlers after the change, and that each of the three handlers imports from src/validation.js.

Out of scope: fixing or improving the validation rules, rewording messages, validating other fields, touching handlers other than the three named, changing response formats, adding dependencies, or adding lint, build or typecheck tooling.

The handler source, the current validation rules, the message strings and the existing test coverage were not supplied; only the commit id and the test command are known. Equivalence of the three copies and the file extension and location of the handlers and tests are unverified.

Assumes the validation in each handler is separable from surrounding logic, meaning it does not depend on other request fields, database lookups such as email uniqueness, or handler-specific context. Any such dependent check stays in the handler and is not part of the shared module.

If the three handlers currently differ in validation rules or error messages for the same value, should the work stop for a decision, or is one handler's variant to be treated as canonical?

Should presence and optionality checks (for example a required-field message, or updateUser skipping an absent field) move into validateEmail and validateName, or remain in the handlers with the shared functions covering only format rules?
If the existing code can report more than one error for a single field, which single message should the validator return, given it returns one message or null?
Is adding characterisation tests for the handlers acceptable where existing tests do not already pin the current messages, or should new tests be limited to the new module?

In that case implementation must stop at the divergence and surface it rather than silently choosing one variant, adding undisclosed parameters, or leaving a handler-specific rule behind.
Requiring validators to have no side effects could conflict with preserving existing behavior if the current validation has observable side effects; the original request does not establish purity.

Requiring that no validation-related regexes, length checks, or message literals remain anywhere in src/handlers is broader than extracting the duplicated rules from the three named handlers, and may conflict with retaining existing presence, optionality, or context-dependent checks.

Declaring any difference between the existing copies an automatic signature conflict and requiring implementation to stop is too categorical. Differences in surrounding checks may still permit shared validators without changing behavior.
Exporting exactly the two named functions prohibits additional exports, which the user did not prohibit.
Comparing the implementations line by line and recording equivalence as a formal precondition adds a mandatory process and deliverable beyond the requested refactor.
